A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Transformers Handle Endogeneity in In-Context Linear Regression. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original transformer-versus-OLS/2SLS simulations measuring prediction and coefficient errors. Appendix C also reports sample-regularity diagnostics and gradient-descent convergence experiments.

after.justification: The original simulations remain, supplemented by multicollinearity, nonlinear-first-stage, and endogeneity-strength experiments and original estimates on a labor-supply dataset in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a ridge-2SLS extension with penalties in both optimization levels, corresponding gradient updates, and p+1 additional second-layer attention heads. This is a limited procedural and architectural extension; the original GD-2SLS construction, pretraining scheme, coefficient extraction, and experimentally trained model remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 extends the previously synthetic-only evaluation to 6,421 Alabama observations from the Angrist–Evans labor-supply dataset. Appendices C.3–C.5 also add multicollinear inputs, neural-network nonlinear first stages, and varying endogeneity strength, retaining the original standard, weak-instrument, quadratic, and underidentified scenarios.

E2.justification: OLS and 2SLS remain the comparators in the retained experiments. V2 additionally evaluates Ridge OLS and Ridge 2SLS in the heavy-multicollinearity comparison in Figure 5b; these regularized comparators were not evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: Added experiments specify collinearity perturbations with variance 10^-6 and regularization parameters set to 1. The real-data protocol compares transformer estimates from 50-observation subsets with full-dataset OLS/2SLS estimates, without known coefficient ground truth. The original training budget, model configuration, and synthetic evaluation metrics are unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices C.3–C.5 add substantial robustness analyses testing transfer to multicollinearity, more complex nonlinear first stages, and changing confounding strength. V1's empirical justification of sample-regularity assumptions, including its 10,000-simulation histograms, is removed. The existing GD convergence and learning-rate analyses remain, moving from C.2 to C.1.

E5.justification: The real-data example newly reports a median and boxplot with interquartile range, whiskers, and outliers across 500 randomly selected subsets. Retained simulation curves still average 500 simulations; no increase in training seeds is reported. The old 10,000-run diagnostic histograms and their empirical quantiles disappear.

E6.justification: The original performance and GD convergence plots are unchanged, but Figures 5–7 add error curves for the new robustness settings. Figure 8 reports a transformer median of -0.091 alongside full-dataset 2SLS and OLS estimates of -0.089 and -0.023. V1's sample-regularity histogram results are removed. These are added or removed findings, not improvements in the original same-setting scores.

T1.justification: Assumption 2 replaces the assumed sample-event conditions with centered instruments, bounded first-stage noise, and linear conditional means, also dropping the former conditional-validity/moment assumption. Theorem 2.1 gains explicit sample-size requirements and population-dependent bounds, supported by new Lemma A.4. Theorem 3.3 and its proof incorporate the revised bound, while Appendix C.2 adds a regularized convergence argument and attention construction.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: transformers can emulate 2SLS with exponential convergence, attain small pretraining excess loss, and generalize to difficult IV scenarios. The claimed first non-asymptotic random-design 2SLS bound is also retained.

C2.justification: Appendices C.2–C.3 connect ridge-2SLS representability with potential robustness to multicollinearity without corresponding pretraining tasks. C.6 interprets the labor-supply estimates as evidence of practical applicability while acknowledging that the true effect is unknown. The earlier weak-instrument mechanism conjecture remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix C.7 newly discloses Windows 11, an RTX 4090, an i9-14900KF, 32 GB DDR5 memory, and approximately 10 hours of training. New experiments also document their data-generation and regularization settings. These disclosures do not establish changes to the existing training procedure.

R1.justification: V2 adds Jin et al. (2025) and Huang et al. (2024), supporting theoretical references including Hsu et al. (2014) and Vershynin (2018), and labor-supply application references. Rudelson and Vershynin (2010) is removed. Overall positioning remains stable; the Peixoto-to-Fonseca citation change refers to the same work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, main section order, and most explanatory prose remain intact. Changes include localized wording corrections, notation clarification, acknowledgements, updated cross-references, and expansion and reorganization of Appendix C. The scientific additions do not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the experimental displays with multicollinearity panels, nonlinear and endogeneity-strength plots, and a real-data boxplot in Figures 5–8. V1 Figure 3's histograms are removed. Main Figures 1–2 are unchanged, and v1 Figures 4–5 are retained and renumbered as v2 Figures 3–4.

improvement.justification: The added robustness tests, ridge comparators, real-data example, and resource disclosures improve empirical support and transparency. However, v2 removes v1's Assumption 2(iv), while Appendix A.1 still infers conditional centering from unconditional IV exogeneity in Equation (27) and uses conditional variance control in Equation (35), without supplying a replacement justification. Because the revised finite-sample and downstream excess-loss guarantees depend on these steps, the empirical gains and theoretical uncertainty prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
